1. Data

The data are the CDC national influenza surveillance series distributed with MIFlu: 966 weekly rows x 7 numeric channels, bit-identical to the author's file (maximum absolute difference 0.000e+00). The split is chronological 70/10/20 — rows 0-675 train, 676-772 validation, 773-965 test (193 rows) — and every window is checked against a containment guard, so a window's input span always ends before its target span starts (minimum admitted test target-start row 773). Standardisation uses a StandardScaler fitted on the training block only.

Why 676/97/193 (70/10/20)? This is the standard protocol of the long-horizon forecasting benchmark family (Informer, AAAI 2023; DLinear, AAAI 2023; PatchTST, ICLR 2023; iTransformer, ICLR 2024) and the split used by the original MIFlu repository. The integer arithmetic is 966 x 0.7 = 676, 966 x 0.2 = 193, remainder 97. We follow it exactly so that the numbers are comparable.

Why (W//16)*16 evaluation windows? This is not a journal requirement. It is a side effect of the original code's DataLoader(batch_size=16, drop_last=True), which discards the final partial batch of test windows: 170 -> 160, 158 -> 144, 146 -> 144, 134 -> 128. The discarded windows are measurably harder (about 1.41x the retained mean), so scoring MIFlu on the cropped set while scoring every other arm on the full set would hand MIFlu an easier test. All 28 arms are therefore scored on the same cropped windows.
Table 1. The dataset, the split and the evaluation windows.
The scaling constants are why a 7-variable aggregate cannot be de-normalised: OT and ILITOTAL live four orders of magnitude apart, so the aggregate is a loss, not a series.
2. Methodology

Two protocols are used, and they are never mixed. (1) Reproduction: 10 repetitions, seeds 2021-2030, validation-selected checkpoint, 7-variable aggregate MSE — the protocol needed to compare with the paper's Table V. (2) Benchmark: 3 seeds (42/43/44), shared windows (W//16)*16 = 160/144/144/128 — the protocol used to compare 28 arms with each other. MIFlu is the only arm that appears under both, and its two numbers are not comparable to each other.
Table 2. The two evaluation protocols. They are never mixed and their numbers are never compared.
MIFlu is the only arm that appears under both protocols; its two numbers answer different questions and are not comparable to each other (see the reproduction section).

Why 3 seeds in the benchmark but 10 in the reproduction? The reproduction follows the paper's protocol (10 repetitions) so that a like-for-like comparison is possible. The benchmark follows the convention of the forecasting literature: PatchTST (ICLR 2023, arXiv:2211.14730) and iTransformer (ICLR 2024) both report three-seed means. Three seeds across 28 arms keeps the matrix at 28 x 4 x 3 = 336 cells, which is tractable on one A100 partition; ten seeds would be 1,120 cells for no gain in the comparisons that are made here.
Table 3. Reproduction: ours vs original paper/repo.
Two [DEVIATION] items are required by top-tier journal standards.

What are the two [DEVIATION] items, and why are they necessary? (1) Checkpoint selection: the original code selects the best epoch on the test set (main_ILI_lora.py, lines 211 and 225). That is data leakage — the test set is the final exam, and a model must not consult it while being chosen. We select on the validation block. (2) The 7-variable metric: the original test loader covers only 1 of the 7 variables (a bug), while Table V is defined on a 7-variable aggregate. We fix the loader. Both deviations are disclosed wherever a reproduction number appears.
Table 4. Benchmark protocol: ours vs the original repo (which uses fix_seed=2021, single seed).
The original paper has no benchmark — this is our contribution.

Why does PTE/PIE use ILITOTAL while MSE uses the 7-variable aggregate? The aggregate is a loss, not a time series: its seven channels have training means from 1.74 (% WEIGHTED ILI) to 493,629 (OT), so averaging them produces a number with no physical unit and no de-normalisation. Peak timing and peak height, by contrast, are statements about a single interpretable series in patient counts. PTE/PIE therefore use ILITOTAL de-normalised with the train-fit scaler (mean 9,439.84, sd 9,003.15 patients). The reproduction keeps the aggregate because Table V is defined on it.
3. Reproduction of MIFlu's Table V

The four-horizon mean is 1.4995 against the paper's 1.4355, i.e. 4.5 % worse, but the mean is the least informative part of the result. The sign flips with the horizon: at L=24 we are 15.4 % better than the paper (1.3045 against 1.542) and at L=36 4.6 % better (1.3561 against 1.422), while at L=48 we are 17.0 % worse (1.6543 against 1.414) and at L=60 23.4 % worse (1.6829 against 1.364). The MAE side shows the same crossover: 0.7482 / 0.7712 / 0.8381 / 0.8596 against 0.726 / 0.779 / 0.757 / 0.719, a four-horizon mean of 0.8043 against 0.7452 (+7.9 %).
Table 5. Reproduction of MIFlu's Table V — the sign crossover. 7-variable aggregate MSE in z-space, 10 repetitions, seeds 2021–2030.

A positive Δ means we are worse than the paper. We win L24 (−15.4 %) and L36 (−4.6 %) and lose L48 (+17.0 %) and L60 (+23.4 %); the 4-horizon mean is +4.5 % on MSE and +7.9 % on MAE. The only defensible claim is “reproduced within 4.5 % on the 4-horizon MSE mean, with a horizon-dependent sign” — never a claim of superiority over the original. Windows (W//16)*16 = 160/144/144/128; A100-SXM4-80GB, partition stingy, CityU HPC Burgundy. Source: ESSAY_VS_REPRODUCTION_TABLE_V.csv.

Two explanations are consistent with this pattern, and the data cannot yet separate them. The first is checkpoint selection: our validation-selected checkpoints are not the same objects as the author's test-selected ones, and a test-selected checkpoint has an advantage that grows with horizon, because longer horizons have more variance to exploit. The second is simply variance: the ten repetitions span 1.201-1.465 at L=24 and 1.401-1.984 at L=60, so a 17 % gap at L=48 and a 23 % gap at L=60 are large but not absurd given that spread — the run that produced 1.6829 at L=60 also produced 1.4108 on a different seed.

The only defensible claim is: reproduced within 4.5 % on the four-horizon MSE mean, with a horizon-dependent sign. It is not a claim of superiority over the original, and it is not “the paper is wrong”.

The per-seed oracle is included because a reproduction claim is only as strong as its provenance. Every later re-export of a MIFlu cell, including the benchmark instance, is gated against that table at |Δ| <= 1e-5 by 05_程序代码/verify_miflu_oracle.py; a cell that does not match is rejected rather than averaged in.

The curves show what the MSE gap is made of. At L=24 the step-0 curve tracks the ground truth through every rise and fall, and the degradation with step is visible but orderly. At L=60 the model still captures the seasonal shape — it is not a broken model — but it systematically under-shoots the three peaks, and the under-shoot is largest at the sharpest peak (the 2017-18 season). That is the visual form of a positive MSE gap at long horizon: the model has learned the seasonality and lost the amplitude.
4. Benchmark 1 — accuracy (28 arms)

The benchmark contains 28 arms across six families: (1) linear (NLinear) — the simplest baseline; (2) transformer (PatchTST, iTransformer) — the current long-horizon state of the art; (3) neural (DNN, CNN, RNN, LSTM, GRU); (4) classical machine learning (gradient boosting, random forest, decision tree, SVR, KNN); (5) LLM-based forecasters (MIFlu, TimeCMA, Qwen-Time, CALF) — the paper's approach and its published competitors; (6) frozen LLM encoders (11 arms: Qwen2.5, DeepSeek-R1-Distill at five sizes, Tencent Hunyuan and ContextPilot) — the question of whether pre-trained language representations transfer to an epidemiological series. The matrix is 28 x 4 horizons x 3 seeds = 336 cells, of which 204 (13 conventional + 3 published LLM-based + DLinear) carry measured A100 provenance and 132 are the encoder cells.

Table 7. The 28-arm benchmark: 7-variable aggregate MSE per horizon and as a four-horizon mean, plus the four-horizon MAE, in z-space. Mean over seeds 42/43/44, on the shared (W//16)*16 windows 160/144/144/128.

Lower is better. Per-horizon MAE is omitted for legibility; it is in 02_数字表格/BENCH_MSE_BY_MODEL_L.csv. DLinear is excluded by project decision (the original paper's Table V already benchmarks it, so it adds no new baseline). The seasonal-naive reference (52-week lag) scores 6.2132 on the same windows, so every one of the 28 arms beats it. Hardware: A100-SXM4-80GB, partition stingy, CityU HPC Burgundy — 204/204 cells of the 17 arms (13 conventional + 3 published LLM-based + DLinear) carry that measured provenance, and the MIFlu and encoder cells were run on the same partition with per-cell manifests on the cluster. Parameter counts are the trained-model totals from BENCH_EFFICIENCY.csv; classical learners and MIFlu are non-parametric in this sense (or not exported) and are left blank.

Three features of the table matter more than the ordering. First, MIFlu is the accuracy champion at 1.5574, followed by PatchTST (1.6621) and NLinear (1.8716): the paper's own model does win once it is placed on the same protocol as everyone else. Second, a linear model with 2,520 parameters is third of 28, ahead of every transformer except PatchTST — a result that should make a reader suspicious of the assumption that architectural sophistication is what buys accuracy on a 966-row series. Third, the spread is large: 1.5574 to 5.6155 is a factor of 3.6, so model choice dominates any hyper-parameter tuning reported in the papers being compared.

Finding F0 — accuracy alone does not identify a deployable model. The top three arms are separated by 20 % of MSE, and the remaining 25 arms span a further 3.0x. A ranking is therefore easy to produce and hard to act on: it says which model fits this test set best, not which model supports the decision the forecast exists for. Benchmarks 2-4 ask the questions the ranking cannot answer.

5. Benchmark 2 — peak skill on the Kramer & Shaman criterion

Peak skill replaces the question “how close is the curve” with the question “does the forecast support a decision”. On ILITOTAL de-normalised to patient counts we compute, per fixed step 0/1/2/3 = 1/2/3/4 weeks ahead, the peak-timing error (PTE, weeks) and the peak-intensity error (PIE, % of the observed peak). A cell passes the Kramer & Shaman criterion only if PTE <= 1 week AND PIE <= 25 % in the same cell. The two halves are a conjunction, and most arms fail one of them even when the other looks excellent.
Table 8. Peak skill per fixed step: PTE (weeks) and PIE (%) on ILITOTAL de-normalised to patient counts, mean over the four horizons; ✓ marks a Kramer & Shaman pass (PTE ≤ 1 week AND PIE ≤ 25 %).

Two arms pass, and they pass differently. NLinear passes all four step-0 cells (4 of 16): mean PTE 1.677 weeks and mean PIE 9.477 % over all 16 cells, with a step-0 PIE of 3.25 % — an order of magnitude inside the criterion. MIFlu also passes 4 of 16, but three of them are step-0 cells (L=48 fails at step 0 with PTE 1.222 weeks) and the fourth is L=48 at step 1; its mean PIE is 26.846 %, i.e. its passes sit close to the 25 % boundary rather than inside it. PatchTST has the best timing (mean PTE 1.240 weeks) but a mean PIE of 32.755 % and 0 passes: it misses the calibration half of the criterion in every cell. Windows 160/144/144/128; seeds 42/43/44; A100-SXM4-80GB, partition stingy, CityU HPC Burgundy.
Table 9. The same criterion cell by cell: every (horizon, step) pair for the three named arms. PASS requires PTE ≤ 1 week AND PIE ≤ 25 % in the same cell.

16 cells per model = 4 horizons × 4 steps, each a mean over seeds 42/43/44. NLinear passes 4 of 16, all at step 0 (PIE 2.4–4.2 %); MIFlu passes 4 of 16 — three at step 0 and one at L=48 step 1, with PIE 18.3–24.8 %, i.e. against the boundary; PatchTST passes none, because its PIE stays in the 26–35 % band at every step. Peak detection: find_peaks(prominence = 0.15 × range, distance = 15) with ±8-week matching — this study's engineering choice, not part of the published criterion. The 1-week / 25 % thresholds are attributed to Kramer & Shaman (2019) but remain [to verify] against the original text.

Two arms pass, and they pass differently. NLinear passes all four step-0 cells (4 of 16), with a mean PTE of 1.68 weeks and a mean PIE of 9.48 % over all 16 cells; at step 0 its mean PIE is 3.2 %, an order of magnitude inside the criterion. MIFlu also passes 4 of 16, but three are step-0 cells and the fourth is L=48 at step 1: at L=48 step 0 its PTE is 1.22 weeks, and its PIE values across the passing cells are 18.3-24.8 %, i.e. against the boundary rather than inside it. PatchTST passes none: its timing is the best in the study (mean PTE 1.24 weeks) but its PIE is 32.8 %, and it misses the calibration half in every cell.

The mechanism is visible in the curves. A model trained to minimise squared error is rewarded for tracking the level and is punished only quadratically for missing a peak; a smooth, slightly conservative forecast is a good MSE strategy and a bad peak strategy, because the peak is the one place where the loss is dominated by a handful of weeks. NLinear, essentially a linear map with a per-window level correction, produces a sharper response at the peak: it over-shoots more often, which costs it MSE, and lands closer to the peak height more often, which is what PIE measures. This is a hypothesis consistent with the data, not a proven mechanism.

Finding F1 — the deployment ordering is not the accuracy ordering. Across all 28 arms, better MSE does go with better calibration (Spearman ρ = +0.74 against mean PIE): the two axes are not independent, and MSE is a useful screen. What fails is the ordering of the frontier. Among the three lowest-MSE arms the calibration order is inverted at both ends — NLinear (3rd on MSE) has the lowest PIE at 9.5 %, MIFlu (1st) sits at 26.8 % and PatchTST (2nd) at 32.8 % — and the pass indicator is negatively rank-correlated with MSE (ρ = -0.43, p = 0.023). The runner-up by MSE passes nothing; the third-best passes every horizon one week ahead. That is the finding a deployment decision turns on, and a leaderboard sorted by MSE cannot express it.
6. Benchmark 3 — the accuracy-efficiency frontier

The Pareto frontier answers a different question from the peak criterion: not “is this model good enough to deploy” but “how much accuracy does each additional parameter buy”. A model is Pareto-optimal if no other model achieves both lower error and fewer parameters. The frontier has exactly two members: NLinear (2,520 parameters, MSE 1.8716) and PatchTST (531,878 parameters, MSE 1.6621). Across the 11 parametric arms, a regression of the four-horizon mean MSE on log10(parameters) gives a slope of +0.1171 with R² = 0.0223.
Table 10. Accuracy–efficiency summary, and the rank association between accuracy and peak skill.

A positive slope means more parameters are associated with a higher (worse) MSE, and R² = 0.0223 means size explains about 2 % of the variance: parameter count is not a useful selection criterion on this dataset. The two Pareto rows should be read as a trade-off, not a ranking — PatchTST spends 211× the parameters for 11.2 % lower MSE. The last two rows keep the peak-skill claim honest: across all 28 arms, better MSE does go with better calibration (ρ = +0.74), so the two axes are not independent; what fails is the ordering of the frontier (the peak-skill tables) and the acceptance verdict, which is negatively rank-correlated with MSE (ρ = -0.43). Windows 160/144/144/128; seeds 42/43/44.

Both signs of that sentence matter. The slope is positive, so more parameters are associated with a higher (worse) MSE; and R² is 2 %, so size explains almost none of the variance. The two Pareto rows then read as a trade-off rather than a ranking: PatchTST spends 211x the parameters of NLinear for 11.2 % lower MSE. Whether that is a good trade depends on the deployment — and, given Finding F1, on whether the deployment needs peak skill, in which case the 11.2 % accuracy advantage buys a model that fails the epidemiological criterion outright.

Finding F2 — parameter count is not a proxy for accuracy. The slope is positive and R² is 0.0223: on this dataset, size is uninformative about accuracy, and what little signal there is points the wrong way. The frontier is a two-model trade-off, not a ranking, and the cheaper member of the frontier is the one that passes the domain criterion at every horizon.
7. Benchmark 4 — statistical significance

The Pareto analysis is descriptive: it says what the trade-off is, and needs no inference. The significance analysis is inferential: it asks whether the 11.2 % difference is distinguishable from seed noise at all. Both are needed, because a trade-off is only worth discussing if the difference being traded is real.

On the 12 matched (horizon x seed) cells we run exact paired sign-flip tests over all 136 pairs of the 17 non-encoder arms (MIFlu and the 11 encoders are outside this family), with Holm-Bonferroni correction, a bootstrap 95 % CI (10,000 resamples) and Cohen's d. 128 of 136 pairs are significant before correction; after proper Holm over 136 pairs none survives, because n = 12 makes the smallest attainable adjusted p 0.066. The pair the Pareto argument needs is NLinear vs PatchTST: mean Δ MSE +0.2095 in PatchTST's favour, NLinear lower in only 2 of 12 cells, raw p = 0.0059, p(Holm) = 0.117, d = 1.15.

Table 11. Paired sign-flip tests on the 12 matched (horizon × seed) cells, Holm-corrected over all 136 pairs (recomputed from the raw p-values). First row: the Pareto pair discussed in the text (bold). Remaining rows: the six smallest p-values, for contrast.

Positive Δ means model A has the larger MSE. All 12 cells are matched (same horizon, same seed), which is only possible because every arm uses seeds 42/43/44. The exported p_holm column was produced with a reverse cumulative minimum, which is not a valid Holm adjustment; the values here are recomputed from p_raw. With n = 12 the smallest attainable raw p is 2/2¹² ≈ 0.00049, so with m = 136 pairs the smallest attainable adjusted p is 0.066 and no pair survives at 0.05 (128/136 are significant before correction). Why the first row is not in the second block: NLinear vs PatchTST has adjusted p = 0.117, the 117th smallest of 136, so a table sorted by significance omits the one comparison the Pareto argument needs. The difference is not resolvable at this sample size; that is a failure to reject, not a demonstration of equivalence (d = 1.15, and PatchTST is lower in 10 of 12 cells).

Why the paired-test table looks like it is about other models: it is sorted by p, and the NLinear-PatchTST pair is the 117th smallest of 136 — a “strongest six” table would silently omit the one comparison the argument needs. The table therefore puts that pair in the first row and the six most significant pairs below it, so both facts are visible at once: before correction most of the roster separates; after correction the study cannot separate any pair — a statement about power, not about the models — and the frontier pair is the one the argument needs.

Finding F3 — the 211x parameter cost is not statistically distinguishable from noise. p(Holm) = 0.117 means we cannot reject equality of the two means at the 5 % level. Three qualifications keep this honest: with n = 12 the smallest attainable p is 2/2¹² ≈ 0.00049; non-significance is a failure to reject, not a demonstration of equivalence; and the effect size is d = 1.15 with PatchTST lower in 10 of 12 cells, so the direction is consistent even though the difference is not resolvable at this sample size. The correct conclusion is not “the models are equal” but “this benchmark does not establish an accuracy advantage for the 211x cost” — which, together with Finding F1, is enough to make NLinear the defensible default.
8. Frozen LLM encoders as feature extractors

The encoder axis asks whether a pre-trained language model is a useful feature extractor for an epidemiological series. Each arm is a frozen encoder plus one shared linear head, trained channel-independently; no encoder weight is updated, and the head is the only trainable part. This is deliberately the charitable version of the idea: if the representation carries usable information, a linear read-out is enough to expose it, and a failure cannot be blamed on fine-tuning instability. 132 of 156 cells are complete (11 arms x 4 horizons x 3 seeds); the 24 missing cells belong to two embedding-only models that cannot emit per-layer hidden states.
Table 12. The 11 frozen-LLM-encoder arms (seed set 42/43/44, four horizons, 12 cells per arm).

Every arm is a frozen encoder plus one shared linear head, trained channel-independently; no encoder weight is updated. Per-arm 7-variable z-space MSE on the shared (W//16)*16 windows and per-step PTE/PIE on ILITOTAL are computed from the 132 exported cells (11 arms x 4 horizons x 3 seeds). The two embedding-only arms and the five excluded arms are listed in the next table.
Table 13. Arms that are not in the roster table, and why.

“Skipped” means the model loads and runs but cannot expose per-layer hidden states, so it cannot feed the adapter — a property of the architecture, not a failure of the method. “Excluded” means the arm never reached a training step.

The result is uniform and negative. The best encoder (Hunyuan-1.8B) reaches 4.7374 and the worst (Qwen2.5-1.5B) 5.2049, i.e. 3.04x to 3.34x the MSE of MIFlu (1.5574), and every one of the 11 is worse than a decision tree (4.3198). None passes the Kramer & Shaman criterion in any cell. The ordering inside the family is not explained by size: a 1.8B model is the best and a 7B model of the same vendor is worse, so whatever the encoders carry, it is not a monotone function of capacity.

Finding F4 — frozen LLM representations do not transfer to this task. Eleven encoders, five model families, 1.5B to 32B parameters, 132 cells: none beats a decision tree and none passes the domain criterion. The negative result is informative because the protocol was designed to give the idea its best chance (frozen features, linear read-out, channel independence) and it still fails; it does not follow that an encoder can never help, but it does mean that a paper claiming a gain from frozen language features on this task owes a mechanism and a control.
9. The ablation ladder: design and current status

The ablation ladder asks where MIFlu's accuracy comes from. The paper's model is a GPT-2 backbone with low-rank adapters (LoRA), a text branch, and a linear head, so the two knobs that could carry the result are (a) the LoRA adaptation and (b) the depth of the stack. The ladder is therefore five variants: no LoRA, and K = 2, 4, 8, 12 transformer layers, each at four horizons and three seeds (5 x 12 = 60 cells), compared against the full K=6 arm already in the benchmark table.

The question each variant answers is worth stating, because “ablation” without a hypothesis is just extra runs. no_lora isolates the frozen backbone: if accuracy survives, the adaptation is not what carries it. K=2 and K=4 test whether depth is needed at all on a 966-row series; K=8 and K=12 test whether extra capacity helps or merely over-fits. The reference arm is the K=6 model already reported, so the ladder contains no duplicated run.
Table 14. The ablation ladder (called Table VIII in the project plan): five variants, 60 cells, and what each one is for.

Each variant is 4 horizons × 3 seeds = 12 cells; five variants = 60 cells; the reference arm is the 12 cells already reported in the benchmark table and is not counted twice. At the snapshot these documents are built from, 27 of 60 cells were complete (driver job 722968) and the per-variant export had not been pulled, so this document reports the design and the completion count and claims no depth trend. The --no-text variant is deliberately not a row: the text tokens sit behind the causal mask and the head reads only the time patches, so --no-text is bit-identical to the full arm — a structural verification (asserted by tests_archive/test_miflu_ablations.py), never an ablation effect.

One ablation result is already established, and it is a negative one about the text branch: the text tokens are appended after the time patches behind a causal mask, and the output head reads only the time-patch positions. Two different text tensors therefore give bit-identical predictions, and --no-text is bit-identical to the full arm with the same seed — asserted by tests_archive/test_miflu_ablations.py, not assumed. In the published architecture the text branch cannot change a number, so a “text ablation” row would be a structural verification, not an effect. That is why the modality claim of the original paper should be read carefully: whatever its text branch contributes, it is not visible in this implementation.

The remaining five variants are not yet reported. At the snapshot these documents are built from, 27 of 60 cells were complete (driver job 722968) and the per-variant export had not been pulled, so this section reports the design and the completion count and claims no depth trend. An earlier internal note that described the ladder as complete at 60/60 and “monotonic” is not supported by any artefact in this repository and has been removed from the reports.

Finding F5 (provisional) — the modality claim is not supported by the architecture as shipped. The text branch is masked out of the prediction path, so --no-text cannot move a number; the depth and LoRA questions remain open until the 60 cells are aggregated. This is reported as a design and a status, not as a result.
10. What the evidence does and does not support

Four claims are supported by the artefacts in this repository: (1) the reproduction lands within 4.5 % of the published four-horizon MSE mean with a horizon-dependent sign; (2) on one common protocol, MIFlu is the accuracy champion of 28 arms and NLinear is third with 2,520 parameters against PatchTST's 531,878; (3) the deployment ordering is not the accuracy ordering — the frontier is inverted on calibration and the pass indicator is negatively rank-correlated with MSE; (4) frozen LLM encoders do not transfer to this task under a protocol designed to favour them.

Five claims are not supported, and the reports do not make them. (1) Superiority over the original: the reproduction is 4.5 % worse on the mean, and the per-horizon wins do not survive as a claim because the protocol differs in two disclosed ways. (2) “MSE and peak skill are unrelated”: they are positively correlated across the roster (ρ = +0.74); the finding is about the frontier, not about independence. (3) “NLinear is the only arm that passes”: MIFlu also passes 4 of 16, by a different route and against the boundary. (4) “PatchTST's advantage is zero”: the test fails to reject equality, which is not the same statement. (5) “The ablation shows a monotonic depth trend”: the ladder is 27/60 and no per-variant number has been aggregated.

The threats to validity are worth naming. The K&S thresholds are attributed to Kramer & Shaman (2019) but remain [to verify] against the original text; the peak detector is this study's engineering choice. The benchmark has one dataset, one country and one target series, so nothing here establishes cross-dataset generality. The significance tests have n = 12, so their resolution is coarse by construction. There is no rolling-origin evaluation yet: every number is from a single chronological split, so a season that falls in the test block is seen once. Finally, the encoder axis is a frozen-feature test; it does not test generation, prompting or fine-tuning, and its negative result must not be over-read.

1. 数据

数据是随 MIFlu 发布的美国 CDC 全国流感监测序列：966 个每周行 x 7 个数值通道，与作者文件逐字节相同（最大绝对差 0.000e+00）。切分为按时间 70/10/20——第 0-675 行训练、676-772 行验证、773-965 行测试（共 193 行）——每个窗口都通过严格包含约束检查，使输入区间总在目标区间开始之前结束（被接纳的测试目标起始行最小下标为 773）。标准化只使用在训练段上拟合的 StandardScaler。

为什么用 676/97/193（70/10/20）？ 这是长跨度预测基准家族的标准协议（Informer, AAAI 2023；DLinear, AAAI 2023；PatchTST, ICLR 2023；iTransformer, ICLR 2024），也是原 MIFlu 仓库使用的切分。整数算术为 966 x 0.7 = 676、966 x 0.2 = 193、余 97。我们完全遵循，以保证数字可比。

为什么用 (W//16)*16 评测窗口？ 这不是期刊要求，而是原代码 DataLoader(batch_size=16, drop_last=True) 的副作用：它会丢弃最后不完整的一批测试窗口，170 -> 160、158 -> 144、146 -> 144、134 -> 128。被丢弃的窗口实测更难（约为保留窗口均值的 1.41 倍），因此若 MIFlu 按裁剪后的集合计分、其他模型按全集计分，就等于给 MIFlu 一个更容易的测试集。所以 28 个模型统一在同一批裁剪窗口上计分。
表 1. 数据集、划分与评测窗口。
这些标准化常数正是 7 变量聚合无法反归一化的原因：OT 与 ILITOTAL 的量级相差四个数量级，所以聚合值是一个损失值，而不是一条序列。
2. 方法
本文使用两套协议，且从不混用。(1) 复现： 10 次重复、种子 2021-2030、验证集选择检查点、7 变量聚合 MSE——这是与论文表 V 比较所需的协议。(2) 基准： 3 个种子（42/43/44）、共享窗口 (W//16)*16 = 160/144/144/128——这是 28 个模型互比所用的协议。MIFlu 是唯一同时出现在两套协议下的模型，它的两个数值彼此不可比较。
表 2. 两套评测协议。二者从不混用，其数值也从不互相比较。
MIFlu 是唯一同时出现在两套协议下的模型；它的两个数值回答不同问题，彼此不可比较（见复现一节）。

为什么基准用 3 个种子而复现用 10 个？ 复现遵循论文协议（10 次重复），以便进行同条件比较。基准遵循预测文献的惯例：PatchTST（ICLR 2023, arXiv:2211.14730）与 iTransformer（ICLR 2024）均报告三种子均值。28 个模型用 3 个种子使矩阵为 28 x 4 x 3 = 336 个单元，在单个 A100 分区上可完成；若用 10 个种子则为 1,120 个单元，而对本文所做的比较没有额外收益。
表 3. 复现：本文 vs 原论文/仓库。
两项 [偏离] 为顶刊标准要求。

两处 [DEVIATION] 是什么，为什么必要？ (1) 检查点选择： 原代码在测试集上选最优 epoch（main_ILI_lora.py 第 211、225 行）。这是数据泄漏——测试集是期末考试，选模型时不能看它。我们改为在验证段上选择。(2) 7 变量指标： 原测试加载器只覆盖 7 个变量中的 1 个（bug），而表 V 定义在 7 变量聚合上。我们修复了加载器。两处偏离凡出现在复现数字处均予披露。

原论文无基准——这是我们的贡献。

为什么 PTE/PIE 用 ILITOTAL 而 MSE 用 7 变量聚合？ 聚合值是一个损失，不是时间序列：七个通道的训练均值从 1.74（% WEIGHTED ILI）到 493,629（OT），把它们平均得到的是一个没有物理单位、也无法反归一化的数。峰值时间与峰值高度则是对单一可解释序列（患者人数）的陈述。因此 PTE/PIE 使用经训练集 scaler 反归一化的 ILITOTAL（均值 9,439.84，标准差 9,003.15 人）。复现保留聚合指标，是因为表 V 如此定义。

Δ 为正表示本文比论文更差。本文在 L24（−15.4 %）与 L36（−4.6 %）更好，在 L48（+17.0 %）与 L60（+23.4 %）更差；4 个跨度的均值在 MSE 上为 +4.5 %、在 MAE 上为 +7.9 %。唯一可辩护的表述是“在 4 个跨度的 MSE 均值上复现到 4.5 % 以内，且符号随跨度翻转”，绝不能说“我们超过了论文”。窗口为 (W//16)*16 = 160/144/144/128；A100-SXM4-80GB、stingy 分区、CityU HPC Burgundy。来源：ESSAY_VS_REPRODUCTION_TABLE_V.csv。

有两种解释与该模式相符，而现有数据尚无法区分。其一是检查点选择：本文用验证集选出的检查点与作者用测试集选出的不是同一类对象，而测试集选出的检查点具有随跨度增长的优势，因为更长跨度有更多方差可利用。其二就是方差：十次重复在 L=24 的范围是 1.201-1.465，在 L=60 是 1.401-1.984，因此在如此离散度下，L=48 的 17 % 与 L=60 的 23 % 差距虽大却并不荒谬——产出 L=60 的 1.6829 的那次运行，在另一个种子上也产出过 1.4108。
唯一可辩护的表述是：在四跨度 MSE 均值上复现到 4.5 % 以内，且符号随跨度翻转。这不是“我们优于原论文”，也不是“论文错了”。
本报告给出逐种子 oracle，因为复现论断的强度不会超过其来源的强度。此后每一次 MIFlu 单元（包括基准实例）的重新导出，都由 05_程序代码/verify_miflu_oracle.py 以 |Δ| <= 1e-5 对照该表把关；不匹配的单元被拒绝，而不是被平均进去。

5. 基准二：Kramer & Shaman 判据下的峰值技巧

6. 基准三：精度—效率前沿

帕累托前沿回答的是与峰值判据不同的问题：不是“这个模型是否好到可以部署”，而是“每增加一些参数买到了多少精度”。若无其他模型同时具有更低误差和更少参数，则该模型是帕累托最优的。前沿恰好两个成员：NLinear（2,520 参数，MSE 1.8716）与 PatchTST（531,878 参数，MSE 1.6621）。在 11 个含参数模型上，把四跨度均值 MSE 对 log10(参数量) 做回归，斜率为 +0.1171，R² = 0.0223。

7. 基准四：统计显著性

发现 F4——冻结 LLM 表征不能迁移到本任务。 11 个编码器、5 个模型家族、1.5B 至 32B 参数、132 个单元：没有一个胜过一个决策树，也没有一个通过领域判据。这一负面结果有信息量，因为协议被设计成给该想法最好的机会（冻结特征、线性读出、通道独立），而它仍然失败；这不能推出编码器永远不可能有帮助，但它确实意味着：任何声称在本任务上从冻结语言特征获得增益的论文，都需要给出机制与对照。
9. 消融阶梯：设计与当前状态
消融阶梯要问的是 MIFlu 的精度从何而来。论文模型是 GPT-2 主干 + 低秩适配（LoRA）+ 文本分支 + 线性头，因此可能承载结果的两个旋钮是 (a) LoRA 适配与 (b) 堆叠深度。阶梯因此为五个变体：去掉 LoRA，以及 K = 2、4、8、12 层，每个变体 4 个跨度、3 个种子（5 x 12 = 60 个单元），与已在基准表中的完整 K=6 臂比较。
每个变体要回答的问题值得写明，因为没有假设的“消融”只是多跑几次。no_lora 隔离出冻结主干：若精度仍在，则适配不是承载它的东西。K=2 与 K=4 检验在这条 966 行序列上是否根本需要深度；K=8 与 K=12 检验额外容量是有帮助还是仅仅过拟合。参考臂即已报告的 K=6 模型，因此阶梯中没有重复运行。

10. 证据支持什么、不支持什么
本仓库的产物支持四项主张：(1) 复现在已发表的四跨度 MSE 均值 4.5 % 以内，且符号随跨度翻转；(2) 在同一协议下，MIFlu 是 28 个模型中的精度冠军，NLinear 以比 PatchTST 少 211 倍的参数排第三；(3) 部署排序不是精度排序——前沿在校准上反转，且通过标记与 MSE 呈负秩相关；(4) 在有利于该想法的协议下，冻结 LLM 编码器不能迁移到本任务。

有五项主张不被支持，报告也不作这些主张。(1) 优于原论文：复现在均值上差 4.5 %，而逐跨度的胜出不能作为主张成立，因为协议在两处已披露的地方不同。(2) “MSE 与峰值技巧无关”：它们在榜单上正相关（ρ = +0.74）；发现针对的是前沿，而不是独立性。(3) “NLinear 是唯一通过的模型”：MIFlu 同样通过 4/16，只是路径不同且贴着边界。(4) “PatchTST 的优势为零”：检验未能拒绝相等，这与“相等”不是同一陈述。(5) “消融显示单调的深度趋势”：阶梯为 27/60，尚未聚合任何逐变体数字。

值得点明效度威胁。K&S 阈值归因于 Kramer & Shaman（2019），但仍标注 [to verify]，待与原文核对；峰值检测器是本研究的工程选择。基准只有一个数据集、一个国家、一条目标序列，因此本文不能确立跨数据集的普适性。显著性检验 n = 12，其分辨率在构造上就是粗的。目前没有滚动原点评测：每个数字都来自单一按时间切分，因此落在测试块中的季节只被看到一次。最后，编码器这一轴是冻结特征测试，不测试生成、提示或微调，其负面结果不可过度解读。

CITY UNIVERSITY OF HONG KONG
Department of Electrical Engineering   ·   FYP Progress Report, Semester A 2026/27
PART A
PART B
1. Project objectives

Problem statement. Influenza forecasting directly affects public-health resource allocation: when to escalate a response, how much capacity to prepare, and when to announce that a season has peaked. Moon et al. (IEEE JBHI 2025) proposed MIFlu, a multimodal model that pairs a GPT-2 time-series encoder with text embeddings, and reported the best accuracy on CDC national influenza data. The paper, however, compares against two simple baselines, reports a single random seed, and selects its checkpoint on the test set — data leakage. A public-health team therefore cannot answer the question that matters: is MIFlu the model we should deploy, and would we know if it were not?
Objectives.

1. Reproduce MIFlu's Table V under a rigorous protocol (10 seeds, validation-based checkpoint selection, 7-variable aggregate MSE) and quantify the gap against the published numbers, including its sign at each horizon.

2. Benchmark 28 forecasting models (13 conventional + 4 LLM-based, MIFlu and 3 published, + 11 frozen LLM encoders) on one protocol, scored on accuracy (MSE/MAE) and on peak-forecasting skill (PTE/PIE under the Kramer & Shaman criterion).
3. Determine which model a public-health team should deploy, and test empirically whether large language models improve epidemiological forecasting at all.

Scope. The project is an empirical evaluation, not a new architecture. Its contribution is the measurement: a leak-free protocol, a 28-arm matrix under one set of windows and seeds, and an evaluation that separates accuracy from deployment value. No new loss function or prompt mechanism is proposed, and none is needed for the claims that are made.
2. Original project planning chart
•  Sep 2026 (Weeks 1-4): data acquisition and verification (966-week CDC series, byte-level check). Milestone: dataset confirmed identical — done.
•  Oct 2026 (Weeks 5-8): MIFlu code reconstruction, reproduction runs (10 seeds x 4 horizons). Milestone: Table V reproduced with a disclosed sign crossover — done.

•  Nov 2026 (Weeks 9-12): 28-model benchmark and frozen-encoder axis; ablation ladder queued; progress report and presentation. Milestone: benchmark complete — benchmark done, ablation 27/60 and running.
•  Dec 2026 - Apr 2027: regional evaluation, rolling-origin evaluation, manuscript, submission. Milestone: submitted manuscript — planned.

The one schedule slip is the ablation ladder: it was planned for early November and is 27/60 at this report. It is a compute-queue delay, not a design change; the regional evaluation is gated behind it and has moved to late November.
3. Background study

Technical background. Influenza forecasting has moved from statistical models (ARIMA, Prophet) to deep learning (LSTM, Transformer) and recently to large language models. MIFlu represents the last group: it fine-tunes a GPT-2 backbone with LoRA adapters on the CDC series and reports the best aggregate accuracy. Its comparison set is thin and its protocol has two problems — test-set checkpoint selection and a single seed — which is exactly the space in which an independent reproduction and a wider benchmark become useful.

Contemporary and societal context. After COVID-19, governments invested heavily in AI-based epidemic forecasting, and agencies such as the WHO and CDC use forecasts to allocate vaccines and antivirals. A forecast is useful to those decisions only if its peak is placed and scaled correctly: a curve that is two weeks late on the peak, or 40 % low on its height, fails the decision even when its average error is small. Yet the literature ranks models by MSE. That gap between the metric and the decision is the problem this project measures.

Gap identified. Three things are missing from the current literature: (1) a reproduction of MIFlu that removes the test-set checkpoint leak; (2) a benchmark wide enough that the linear and classical baselines are represented; (3) an evaluation on the criterion public health actually applies, next to the criterion the literature reports. This project supplies all three.
4. Methodology

Design. Two protocols, never mixed. The reproduction protocol (10 seeds, 2021-2030; validation-selected checkpoint; 7-variable aggregate MSE) exists to compare with the paper's Table V. The benchmark protocol (3 seeds 42/43/44; shared windows (W//16)*16 = 160/144/144/128; one metric) exists to compare 28 models with each other. MIFlu is the only arm under both, and its two numbers are not comparable.
Table 1. Reproduction: ours vs original paper/repo.
Two [DEVIATION] items are required by top-tier journal standards.

Two deliberate deviations. (1) Checkpoint selection: the original code selects the best epoch on the test set (main_ILI_lora.py, lines 211 and 225), which is data leakage; we select on validation. (2) The 7-variable metric: the original test loader covers only 1 of 7 variables (a bug), while Table V is defined on the 7-variable aggregate; we fix the loader. Both are disclosed wherever a reproduction number appears.

Metrics and definitions. Horizon L = weeks predicted ahead (input window T = 104 weeks). Step s = which predicted week is scored (step 0 = one week ahead). PTE (peak timing error) = |predicted peak week - observed peak week| in weeks; PIE (peak intensity error) = |predicted - observed peak| / observed peak x 100 %. A cell passes the Kramer & Shaman criterion only if PTE <= 1 week and PIE <= 25 %; the thresholds are attributed to Kramer & Shaman (2019) and are marked [to verify] against the original text. The peak detector (find_peaks(prominence = 0.15 x range, distance = 15), ±8-week matching) is this project's engineering choice, not part of the published criterion. PTE/PIE use ILITOTAL de-normalised to patient counts, because the 7-variable aggregate is a loss, not a series, and cannot be de-normalised.

Design impact in a broader context. The evaluation is deliberately split into two questions that a deployment actually faces: how accurate is the curve (MSE) and can the forecast support a decision (PTE/PIE). Keeping them separate matters because they can rank models differently; a single leaderboard that collapses them would hide the choice. The benchmark is also built to be re-runnable: every cell records its GPU, partition, node and job id, so a public-health team can audit the numbers rather than trust them. That is a small contribution to reproducibility in a field where published forecasting results are rarely re-derived.
6. Progress
Work completed this semester.
•  Data verification: 966-week CDC series confirmed bit-identical to the author's file (SHA-256, max|diff| = 0); split 676/97/193 and the containment guard verified.
•  Code reconstruction: 17 fidelity fixes (RevIN, LayerNorm, three dropouts, drop_last, single-variable batch, seed, epsilon, and others), each recorded in the deviation ledger.
•  Reproduction: 40 runs (10 seeds x 4 horizons), every cell gated against the per-seed oracle at |Δ| <= 1e-5.

•  Benchmark: 28 models x 4 horizons x 3 seeds = 336 cells; 204 of them (the 17 conventional arms) carry recorded per-cell A100 provenance, and the 132 encoder cells ran on the same partition with per-cell manifests on the cluster.
•  Encoder axis: 11 frozen encoders x 12 cells = 132 cells, MSE and PTE/PIE aggregated.
•  Analysis: MSE/MAE, PTE/PIE, the Kramer & Shaman criterion, a Pareto frontier, a log-parameter regression, and 136 Holm-corrected paired tests.
•  Ablation ladder: designed, implemented behind flags, 27/60 cells complete at this report.
•  Documentation: six reports (DOCX + PDF, EN + ZH) generated from the CSVs with assertions.
Reproduction result (7-variable aggregate MSE, 10-seed mean):
Table 2. Reproduction of MIFlu's Table V — the sign crossover. 7-variable aggregate MSE in z-space, 10 repetitions, seeds 2021–2030.

A positive Δ means we are worse than the paper. We win L24 (−15.4 %) and L36 (−4.6 %) and lose L48 (+17.0 %) and L60 (+23.4 %); the 4-horizon mean is +4.5 % on MSE and +7.9 % on MAE. The only defensible claim is “reproduced within 4.5 % on the 4-horizon MSE mean, with a horizon-dependent sign” — never a claim of superiority over the original. Windows (W//16)*16 = 160/144/144/128; A100-SXM4-80GB, partition stingy, CityU HPC Burgundy. Source: ESSAY_VS_REPRODUCTION_TABLE_V.csv.

The paper reports 1.542 / 1.422 / 1.414 / 1.364 (mean 1.4355). We obtain 1.3045 / 1.3561 / 1.6543 / 1.6829 (mean 1.4995), i.e. 4.5 % worse on the mean, with a sign crossover 2-2: better at L=24 and L=36, worse at L=48 and L=60. The MAE side behaves the same way (0.8043 against 0.7452, +7.9 %).

Conclusion (reproduction). The reproduction is within 4.5 % on the four-horizon mean, with a horizon-dependent sign — a reproduction, not an improvement. Reporting only the mean would have hidden the structure, and the two disclosed deviations (validation checkpoint, 7-variable metric) mean the per-horizon wins cannot be claimed as superiority.
Benchmark result (28 arms, 3 seeds, shared windows):

Table 3. The 28-arm benchmark: 7-variable aggregate MSE per horizon and as a four-horizon mean, plus the four-horizon MAE, in z-space. Mean over seeds 42/43/44, on the shared (W//16)*16 windows 160/144/144/128.

Lower is better. Per-horizon MAE is omitted for legibility; it is in 02_数字表格/BENCH_MSE_BY_MODEL_L.csv. DLinear is excluded by project decision (the original paper's Table V already benchmarks it, so it adds no new baseline). The seasonal-naive reference (52-week lag) scores 6.2132 on the same windows, so every one of the 28 arms beats it. Hardware: A100-SXM4-80GB, partition stingy, CityU HPC Burgundy — 204/204 cells of the 17 arms (13 conventional + 3 published LLM-based + DLinear) carry that measured provenance, and the MIFlu and encoder cells were run on the same partition with per-cell manifests on the cluster. Parameter counts are the trained-model totals from BENCH_EFFICIENCY.csv; classical learners and MIFlu are non-parametric in this sense (or not exported) and are left blank.

MIFlu is the accuracy champion at 1.5574, followed by PatchTST (1.6621) and NLinear (1.8716); the spread across all 28 arms is 1.5574 to 5.6155, a factor of 3.6. The published LLM-based competitors are beaten by a nearest-neighbour baseline (KNN 3.7854 vs Qwen-Time 5.2557 and CALF 5.5785), and the 11 frozen encoders occupy the 4.74-5.20 band.

Finding F0 — accuracy alone does not identify a deployable model. The ranking is easy to produce and hard to act on: it says which model fits this test set best, not which model supports the decision the forecast exists for. The next three analyses ask the questions the ranking cannot answer.
Peak-skill result (PTE/PIE, Kramer & Shaman criterion; the grid shows the three named arms cell by cell):
Table 4. The same criterion cell by cell: every (horizon, step) pair for the three named arms. PASS requires PTE ≤ 1 week AND PIE ≤ 25 % in the same cell.

16 cells per model = 4 horizons × 4 steps, each a mean over seeds 42/43/44. NLinear passes 4 of 16, all at step 0 (PIE 2.4–4.2 %); MIFlu passes 4 of 16 — three at step 0 and one at L=48 step 1, with PIE 18.3–24.8 %, i.e. against the boundary; PatchTST passes none, because its PIE stays in the 26–35 % band at every step. Peak detection: find_peaks(prominence = 0.15 × range, distance = 15) with ±8-week matching — this study's engineering choice, not part of the published criterion. The 1-week / 25 % thresholds are attributed to Kramer & Shaman (2019) but remain [to verify] against the original text.

NLinear and MIFlu each pass 4 of 16 cells, but differently: NLinear passes all four step-0 cells with a PIE of 3.2 %, while MIFlu's four passes sit at PIE 18.3-24.8 %, against the 25 % boundary, and it misses L=48 at step 0. PatchTST passes none: its timing is the best in the study (mean PTE 1.24 weeks) but its PIE is 32.8 %.

Finding F1 — the deployment ordering is not the accuracy ordering. Across all 28 arms, better MSE does go with better calibration (Spearman ρ = +0.74 against mean PIE), so MSE is a useful screen; but the frontier is ordered the other way round. Among the three lowest-MSE arms the calibration order is inverted at both ends (NLinear 9.5 %, MIFlu 26.8 %, PatchTST 32.8 %), and the pass indicator is negatively rank-correlated with MSE (ρ = -0.43, p = 0.023). The runner-up by MSE passes nothing; the third-best passes every horizon one week ahead.

Step-0 peak skill for the three named arms. Left: peak-timing error (weeks) at step 0, mean over the four horizons, against the 1-week threshold (dashed). Right: peak-intensity error (%) at step 0 against the 25 % threshold (dashed). Green = inside the threshold, red = outside. MIFlu (0.35 wk, 18.9 %) and NLinear (0.21 wk, 3.2 %) stay inside both thresholds at the mean level, while PatchTST (0.68 wk, 30.6 %) misses the intensity half — the visual form of the decoupling between a good average error and a calibrated peak. Seeds 42/43/44; windows (W//16)*16 = 160/144/144/128.

Efficiency and significance. Across the 11 parametric arms, MSE against log10(parameters) has slope +0.1171 and R² = 0.0223: size explains about 2 % of the variance and its sign is unfavourable. The Pareto set is exactly {NLinear, 2,520 parameters; PatchTST, 531,878 parameters}, i.e. 211x the parameters for 11.2 % lower MSE. On the 12 matched cells of the 17 non-encoder arms, 128 of 136 pairs are significant before correction; after proper Holm none survives (smallest attainable adjusted p 0.066), and the NLinear-PatchTST pair has p(Holm) = 0.117.

Table 5. Paired sign-flip tests on the 12 matched (horizon × seed) cells, Holm-corrected over all 136 pairs (recomputed from the raw p-values). First row: the Pareto pair discussed in the text (bold). Remaining rows: the six smallest p-values, for contrast.

Positive Δ means model A has the larger MSE. All 12 cells are matched (same horizon, same seed), which is only possible because every arm uses seeds 42/43/44. The exported p_holm column was produced with a reverse cumulative minimum, which is not a valid Holm adjustment; the values here are recomputed from p_raw. With n = 12 the smallest attainable raw p is 2/2¹² ≈ 0.00049, so with m = 136 pairs the smallest attainable adjusted p is 0.066 and no pair survives at 0.05 (128/136 are significant before correction). Why the first row is not in the second block: NLinear vs PatchTST has adjusted p = 0.117, the 117th smallest of 136, so a table sorted by significance omits the one comparison the Pareto argument needs. The difference is not resolvable at this sample size; that is a failure to reject, not a demonstration of equivalence (d = 1.15, and PatchTST is lower in 10 of 12 cells).
Finding F2 (efficiency). Parameter count is not a proxy for accuracy: the slope is positive and R² is 0.0223. The frontier is a two-model trade-off, not a ranking.

Finding F3 (significance). The 211x cost buys an 11.2 % MSE difference that this benchmark cannot resolve at n = 12. This is a failure to reject equality, not a proof of equivalence (d = 1.15; PatchTST is lower in 10 of 12 cells), so the defensible conclusion is “no accuracy advantage is established for the 211x cost”, which together with F1 makes NLinear the defensible default.

Accuracy–efficiency Pareto frontier. x = parameter count (log scale), y = 4-horizon mean 7-variable z-space MSE; the step line is the Pareto set {NLinear, 2,520 parameters; PatchTST, 531,878 parameters}. PatchTST spends 211× the parameters of NLinear for 11.2 % lower MSE; the fitted slope of MSE against log₁₀(parameters) is +0.1171 with R² = 0.0223, i.e. size explains ~2 % of the variance and the sign is positive. Windows: shared (W//16)*16 = 160/144/144/128; seeds 42/43/44. Reproduced by plot_pareto.py. Hardware: A100-SXM4-80GB | partition stingy | CityU HPC Burgundy.

Frozen LLM encoders. Eleven encoders (Qwen2.5-1.5B, five DeepSeek-R1-Distill sizes, Hunyuan-1.8B/4B/7B, ContextPilot-8B/14B), each frozen with one shared linear head, 132 of 156 cells. The best is Hunyuan-1.8B at 4.7374 and the worst Qwen2.5-1.5B at 5.2049, i.e. 3.04x to 3.34x the MSE of MIFlu; every one is worse than a decision tree, and none passes the Kramer & Shaman criterion in any cell.

Finding F4 — frozen LLM representations do not transfer to this task. The protocol was built to give the idea its best chance (frozen features, linear read-out, channel independence) and it still fails. This does not prove that an encoder can never help, but it does mean that a claim of gain from frozen language features on this task owes a mechanism and a control.

Ablation ladder (Table VIII in the project plan). Five variants — no LoRA, and K = 2, 4, 8, 12 layers — at four horizons and three seeds (60 cells), compared against the full K=6 arm already in the benchmark table. The ladder answers where MIFlu's accuracy comes from: the LoRA adaptation or the depth of the stack. At this report 27 of 60 cells are complete, so no depth trend is claimed. One result is already established: the text tokens sit behind the causal mask and the head reads only the time patches, so --no-text is bit-identical to the full arm — a structural verification (asserted by tests_archive/test_miflu_ablations.py), not an ablation effect.

Finding F5 (provisional). The text branch is masked out of the prediction path, so the multimodal claim is not supported by the architecture as shipped; the depth and LoRA questions remain open until the 60 cells are aggregated. This is reported as a design and a status, not as a result.

Problems encountered. (1) The original code selects its checkpoint on the test set and scores only 1 of 7 variables in the test loader; both were identified and fixed, and are disclosed as deviations. (2) The evaluation-window rule is a side effect of drop_last=True; adopting it for all arms was necessary to avoid handing MIFlu an easier test. (3) Eight engineering defects were found in the training pipeline (seed not reaching the LLM path, snapshot cloning the frozen encoder, two cache layouts, a non-atomic lock); seven are fixed and one remains open as an operational risk. (4) The ablation ladder has slipped from early November to late November because of queue contention on the shared A100 partition.
7. Summary of objectives addressed and results achieved to date
Table 6. Objectives addressed and results achieved to date
Percentages are estimates of the work completed against each objective as of 3 November 2026.
8. Work schedule and expected results for the next one to two months
Table 7. Work schedule and expected results for the next one to two months
Dates are targets, not commitments; GPU-hour estimates are measured where stated and modelled otherwise.

Risks and mitigation. (1) Queue contention on the shared A100 partition is the reason the ablation slipped; the ladder is submitted as one 60-cell job so it cannot be starved cell by cell. (2) Criterion attribution: the 1-week / 25 % thresholds are marked [to verify] and will be checked against the Kramer & Shaman text before submission; the peak detector is stated as our own choice, so a reader can separate the criterion from the implementation. (3) Single dataset: the regional and rolling-origin evaluations are the mitigation, and if they do not finish in time the paper will state the limitation rather than generalise. (4) Scope: if the ablation or Table VI is still incomplete at submission, the manuscript reports them as design and status, exactly as this report does — no trend, no fabricated number.

The manuscript draft is already written against these results (IEEE structure, EN and ZH; a single-column review draft until submission); the remaining work is to fold in the ablation ladder, the regional table and, if the budget allows, the rolling-origin evaluation. The submission target is IEEE JBHI, with a CCF-B venue as the alternative if the rolling-origin results arrive in time.

PART A
PART B
1. 项目目标

问题陈述。 流感预测直接影响公共卫生资源分配：何时升级响应、准备多少床位与疫苗、何时宣布某季已过峰值。Moon 等（IEEE JBHI 2025）提出 MIFlu——一个把 GPT-2 时间序列编码器与文本嵌入结合的多模态模型——并在 CDC 全国流感数据上报告了最佳精度。但该论文只与两个简单基线比较、只报告单一随机种子，且在测试集上选择检查点——这是数据泄漏。因此公共卫生团队无法回答真正重要的问题：MIFlu 是不是我们该部署的模型？如果不是，我们能否知道？
目标。
1. 用严格协议复现 MIFlu 的表 V（10 个种子、验证集选择检查点、7 变量聚合 MSE），量化与已发表数值的差距，包括每个跨度上的符号。
2. 在同一协议上基准评估 28 个预测模型（13 个传统模型 + 4 个基于 LLM 的预测器（MIFlu 与 3 个已发表）+ 11 个冻结 LLM 编码器），同时用精度（MSE/MAE）与峰值预测技巧（Kramer & Shaman 判据下的 PTE/PIE）计分。
3. 确定公共卫生团队应部署哪个模型，并用实验检验大语言模型是否真的改善流行病学预测。
范围。 本项目是实证评估，不是新架构。其贡献在于测量：无泄漏的协议、在同一窗口与种子下的 28 模型矩阵，以及把精度与部署价值分开的评估。本文不提出新的损失函数或提示机制，所主张的结论也不需要它们。
2. 原始项目规划图
•  2026 年 9 月（第 1-4 周）： 数据获取与验证（966 周 CDC 序列，逐字节校验）。里程碑：数据集确认一致——已完成。
•  2026 年 10 月（第 5-8 周）： MIFlu 代码重建、复现实验（10 个种子 x 4 个跨度）。里程碑：表 V 复现完成，并披露符号交叉——已完成。
•  2026 年 11 月（第 9-12 周）： 28 模型基准与冻结编码器维度；消融阶梯排队；进度报告与汇报。里程碑：基准完成——基准已完成，消融 27/60 运行中。
•  2026 年 12 月–2027 年 4 月： 区域评测、滚动原点评测、手稿、投稿。里程碑：已投稿手稿——计划中。
唯一的进度滑移是消融阶梯：原计划 11 月初完成，本报告时为 27/60。这是算力排队延迟，不是设计变更；区域评测排在其后，已移至 11 月下旬。
3. 背景研究
技术背景。 流感预测已从统计模型（ARIMA、Prophet）发展到深度学习（LSTM、Transformer），再到最近的大语言模型。MIFlu 属于最后一类：用 LoRA 适配器在 CDC 序列上微调 GPT-2 主干，并报告最佳聚合精度。它的比较集很薄，协议有两个问题——测试集选检查点与单一种子——而这正是独立复现与更广基准能发挥作用的空间。
当代与社会背景。 新冠疫情后，各国政府大量投资 AI 疫情预测，WHO 与 CDC 等机构用预测分配疫苗与抗病毒药物。只有当峰值的位置与幅度都正确时，预测才对这类决策有用：一条把峰值判断晚两周、或把峰值高度低估 40 % 的曲线，即使平均误差很小，也已经使决策失败。然而文献仍按 MSE 给模型排名。指标与决策之间的这道鸿沟，正是本项目要测量的对象。
识别的空白。 现有文献缺三样东西：(1) 一个移除测试集检查点泄漏的 MIFlu 复现；(2) 一个宽到足以包含线性与经典基线的基准；(3) 在公共卫生真正使用的判据上、与文献报告的判据并列的评估。本项目三者兼备。
4. 方法
设计。 两套协议，从不混用。复现协议（10 个种子 2021-2030；验证集选择检查点；7 变量聚合 MSE）用于与论文表 V 比较。基准协议（3 个种子 42/43/44；共享窗口 (W//16)*16 = 160/144/144/128；同一指标）用于 28 个模型互比。MIFlu 是唯一同时出现在两套协议下的模型，其两个数值不可比较。

两处故意偏离。 (1) 检查点选择：原代码在测试集上选最优 epoch（main_ILI_lora.py 第 211、225 行），这是数据泄漏；我们改用验证集。(2) 7 变量指标：原测试加载器只覆盖 7 个变量中的 1 个（bug），而表 V 定义在 7 变量聚合上；我们修复加载器。两处偏离凡出现复现数字处均予披露。

指标与定义。 跨度 L = 预测未来周数（输入窗口 T = 104 周）。步 s = 计分第几个预测周（步 0 = 提前一周）。PTE（峰值时间误差）= |预测峰值周 - 观测峰值周|（周）；PIE（峰值强度误差）= |预测 - 观测峰值| / 观测峰值 x 100 %。只有 PTE <= 1 周且 PIE <= 25 % 时该格才通过 Kramer & Shaman 判据；阈值归因于 Kramer & Shaman（2019），并标注 [to verify] 待与原文核对。峰值检测器（find_peaks(prominence = 0.15 x range, distance = 15)，±8 周匹配）是本项目的工程选择，不是已发表判据的一部分。PTE/PIE 使用反归一化为患者人数的 ILITOTAL，因为 7 变量聚合是损失值而不是序列，无法反归一化。
更广背景下的设计影响。 评估被有意拆成部署真正面对的两个问题：曲线有多准（MSE）与预测能否支持决策（PTE/PIE）。把它们分开很重要，因为它们可能给出不同的排序；把二者合并成单一榜单会隐藏这个选择。基准也被设计为可重跑：每个单元记录 GPU、分区、节点与作业号，因此公共卫生团队可以审计这些数字，而不是只能相信它们。在一个已发表预测结果很少被重新推导的领域里，这是对可复现性的一点贡献。

峰值技巧结果（PTE/PIE，Kramer & Shaman 判据；下表逐格展示三个具名模型）：

每模型 16 格 = 4 个跨度 × 4 个步，每格为种子 42/43/44 的均值。NLinear 通过 4/16，全部在步 0（PIE 2.4–4.2 %）；MIFlu 通过 4/16——三个在步 0、一个在 L=48 步 1，PIE 为 18.3–24.8 %，即贴着边界；PatchTST 一个都不通过，因为其 PIE 在每个步都停在 26–35 % 区间。峰值检测：find_peaks(prominence = 0.15 × range, distance = 15) 与 ±8 周匹配——本研究的工程选择，不是已发表判据的一部分。1 周 / 25 % 阈值归因于 Kramer & Shaman (2019)，但仍标注 [to verify]，待与原文核对。
NLinear 与 MIFlu 各通过 4/16，但方式不同：NLinear 通过全部四个步 0 单元，PIE 为 3.2 %；MIFlu 的四个通过点 PIE 为 18.3-24.8 %，贴着 25 % 边界，且在 L=48 步 0 失败。PatchTST 一个都不通过：它的时序是本研究最准的（均值 PTE 1.24 周），但 PIE 为 32.8 %。

发现 F1——部署排序不是精度排序。 在全部 28 个模型上，MSE 更好确实伴随校准更好（对均值 PIE 的 Spearman ρ = +0.74），所以 MSE 是有用的筛选；但前沿的排序正好相反。MSE 最低的三个模型中，校准排序完全反转（NLinear 9.5 %、MIFlu 26.8 %、PatchTST 32.8 %），且通过标记与 MSE 呈负秩相关（ρ = -0.43，p = 0.023）。MSE 第二名一个都不通过；第三名通过每个跨度的提前一周。

冻结 LLM 编码器。 11 个编码器（Qwen2.5-1.5B、五个尺寸的 DeepSeek-R1-Distill、Hunyuan-1.8B/4B/7B、ContextPilot-8B/14B），每个冻结后接一个共享线性头，156 个单元中完成 132 个。最好的是 Hunyuan-1.8B，4.7374；最差的是 Qwen2.5-1.5B，5.2049，即 MIFlu 的 3.04 至 3.34 倍；每一个都差于决策树，且没有任何一个在任何单元通过 Kramer & Shaman 判据。
发现 F4——冻结 LLM 表征不能迁移到本任务。 协议被设计成给该想法最好的机会（冻结特征、线性读出、通道独立），而它仍然失败。这不能证明编码器永远不可能有帮助，但它确实意味着：任何声称在本任务上从冻结语言特征获得增益的主张，都需要给出机制与对照。

消融阶梯（项目计划中的表 VIII）。 五个变体——去掉 LoRA，以及 K = 2、4、8、12 层——在 4 个跨度与 3 个种子上共 60 个单元，与已在基准表中的完整 K=6 臂比较。阶梯回答 MIFlu 的精度从何而来：LoRA 适配，还是堆叠深度。本报告时 60 个单元中完成 27 个，因此不声明任何深度趋势。有一项结果已经确立：文本 token 位于因果掩码之后、输出头只读时间分片，因此 --no-text 与完整臂逐位相同——这是结构验证（由 tests_archive/test_miflu_ablations.py 断言），不是消融效应。
发现 F5（暂定）。 文本分支位于预测路径之外，因此按已交付的架构，多模态主张得不到支持；深度与 LoRA 的问题要等 60 个单元聚合后才能回答。此处报告的是设计与状态，不是结果。

遇到的问题。 (1) 原代码在测试集上选检查点，且测试加载器只对 7 个变量中的 1 个计分；两者均已识别并修复，并作为偏离披露。(2) 评测窗口规则是 drop_last=True 的副作用；为所有模型统一采用它是必要的，否则就等于给 MIFlu 一个更容易的测试。(3) 训练流水线中发现八项工程缺陷（种子未进入 LLM 路径、快照克隆了冻结编码器、两种缓存布局、非原子锁）；七项已修复，一项作为运行风险仍未解决。(4) 消融阶梯因共享 A100 分区排队从 11 月初滑至 11 月下旬。

ieee_manuscript_en.docx.text: Ranking by MSE Is Not Ranking for Deployment: A 28‑Model Reproduction and Benchmark of Influenza Forecasting

Author Name, Member, IEEE — Department of Electrical Engineering, City University of Hong Kong
Supervisor: Prof. Katie Chan — Assessor: Name
(Draft: author block and funding note are placeholders.)

Abstract—Influenza forecasts exist to support decisions, but the literature ranks them by mean squared error. We report an independent reproduction of MIFlu (Moon et al., IEEE JBHI 2025) on the CDC national influenza series (966 weekly rows, 7 channels, bit-identical to the author's file) and a 28-model benchmark the original work does not contain: 13 conventional forecasters, four LLM-based forecasters (MIFlu and three published ones), and 11 frozen large-language-model encoders. The reproduction lands within 4.5 % of the published four-horizon MSE mean (1.4995 against 1.4355) with a horizon-dependent sign: better at L=24 and L=36, worse at L=48 and L=60. On one common protocol (seeds 42/43/44; shared windows (W//16)*16 = 160/144/144/128) the accuracy champion is MIFlu (1.5574), ahead of PatchTST (1.6621) and NLinear (1.8716), and the spread across the roster is a factor of 3.6. On the epidemiological acceptance criterion of Kramer & Shaman (peak-timing error <= 1 week and peak-intensity error <= 25 % on ILITOTAL de-normalised to patient counts), NLinear and MIFlu each pass 4 of 16 cells, but differently: NLinear passes all four step-0 cells with a peak-intensity error of 3.2 %, while MIFlu's passes sit at 18.3-24.8 %, against the boundary. PatchTST passes none: its timing is the best in the study (mean 1.240 weeks) but its intensity error is 32.8 %. Accuracy and calibration are positively rank-correlated across all 28 arms (Spearman rho = +0.74), so MSE is a useful screen; but the frontier is ordered the other way round, and the pass indicator is negatively rank-correlated with MSE (rho = -0.43, p = 0.023). Parameter count does not resolve the choice: the slope of MSE against log10(parameters) is +0.1171 with R2 = 0.0223, the Pareto set is {NLinear, 2,520 parameters; PatchTST, 531,878 parameters}, and the 211x parameter cost buys an 11.2 % MSE difference that does not survive Holm correction over the 136 pairs (p = 0.117; with n = 12 no pair can). None of the 11 frozen encoders passes the criterion, and every one is worse than a decision tree. We argue that the acceptance criterion should be reported next to MSE, and that an MSE-sorted leaderboard can point a deployment decision the wrong way.
Index Terms—Influenza forecasting, reproduction study, benchmark, peak-timing error, peak-intensity error, evaluation protocol, model selection, frozen language-model encoders.

Influenza forecasting exists to support decisions: when to escalate a response, how much capacity to prepare, and when to announce that a season has peaked. The loss behind those decisions is not squared error. A forecast that is two weeks late on the peak, or 40 % low on its height, has failed the decision even if its average error is small; conversely, a forecast with a slightly larger average error but a well-placed, well-scaled peak can be the more useful object. Yet the literature's default ranking metric remains MSE, and model selection follows it.

This paper tests that default on its own terms. We reproduce MIFlu (Moon et al., IEEE JBHI 2025), the current multimodal state of the art on CDC national influenza data, after removing the data leakage in its checkpoint selection; we place it in a 28-model benchmark under one set of windows and seeds; and we score every arm twice — once on the metric the literature reports (MSE) and once on the criterion public health applies (the Kramer & Shaman peak criterion). The two scorings do not agree, and the disagreement is systematic rather than marginal.

Contributions. (1) A leak-free reproduction of MIFlu that reports the per-horizon sign rather than a single mean, and therefore reports a crossover instead of an improvement. (2) A 28-arm benchmark under one protocol — 13 conventional forecasters, 4 LLM-based (MIFlu and 3 published), forecasters, and 11 frozen LLM encoders — with windows, seeds, metric and checkpoint rule held identical. (3) The finding that the deployment ordering is not the accuracy ordering: the frontier is inverted on peak calibration, and the acceptance verdict is negatively rank-correlated with MSE. (4) A parameter-cost and significance analysis showing that the 211x cost of the accuracy runner-up buys a difference this benchmark cannot resolve.

Long-horizon forecasting architectures. PatchTST (Nie et al., ICLR 2023) patches the input series and uses channel independence, and reports three-seed means over standard benchmarks; iTransformer (Liu et al., ICLR 2024) inverts the attention axis and does the same. Zeng et al. (AAAI 2023) argued that a linear model is competitive with transformer forecasters, a claim our benchmark reproduces in the influenza setting: NLinear is third of 28 arms with three orders of magnitude fewer parameters than the accuracy champion.

Epidemiological evaluation. Kramer & Shaman (2019) established the criterion this paper adopts: a forecast is useful only if its peak-timing error is at most one week and its peak-intensity error at most 25 %. The epidemiological literature scores per fixed forecast step; the machine-learning literature scores per horizon. We report both, because they are not the same object: a model can win on one and lose on the other.

Frozen foundation-model features. A frozen encoder with a small trained head is a strong baseline for non-text modalities, and MIFlu itself relies on a frozen GPT-2 backbone with a textual prompt and low-rank adaptation. Whether the choice of encoder matters at the scale of a 966-row epidemiological series has not been established. Section VI-F reports that experiment: eleven encoders, one shared linear head, and a negative result.

Reproduction and benchmark studies. Reproduction work is increasingly recognised as a contribution in its own right, because a benchmark is only as useful as its protocol. Our contribution is of that kind: we do not propose a new architecture, we make the existing comparison honest and then measure what the honest comparison says.

The data are the CDC national influenza surveillance series distributed with MIFlu: 966 weekly rows and 7 numeric channels (% WEIGHTED ILI, % UNWEIGHTED ILI, AGE 0-4, AGE 5-24, ILITOTAL, NUM. OF PROVIDERS, OT). The local file was verified bit-identical to the author's released file (maximum absolute difference 0.000e+00) before any model was trained, because a single mis-joined week would move every number in this paper. The split is chronological 70/10/20 — rows 0-675 training, 676-772 validation, 773-965 test — with a strict containment guard so that a window's input span lies entirely before its target span; the minimum admitted test target-start row is 773. Standardisation uses a StandardScaler fitted on the training block only (ILITOTAL mean 9,439.84 patients, sd 9,003.15; OT mean 493,629).

The scaling constants decide the metric design. Seven channels whose training means span 1.74 to 493,629 cannot be averaged into a quantity with a physical unit: the 7-variable aggregate is a loss, not a series, and it cannot be de-normalised into patient counts. Peak-skill metrics therefore use ILITOTAL alone.

The reproduction uses 10 repetitions with seeds 2021-2030, matching the original author, and validation-selected checkpoints. The benchmark uses 3 seeds, 42/43/44, for every arm, and the same checkpoint rule. They are separate experiments and their numbers are never compared; MIFlu appears under both because a reproduction and a benchmark row impose incompatible requirements, and only the reproduction instance is quoted as a reproduction.

MIFlu's own loader uses DataLoader(batch_size=16, drop_last=True), which discards the final partial batch: 170→160, 158→144, 146→144, 134→128. The discarded windows are measurably harder (1.3929–1.4423 MSE, i.e. ~1.41× the retained mean), so scoring MIFlu on 160/144/144/128 while scoring every other arm on 170/158/146/134 would hand MIFlu an easier test set. All 17 arms are therefore scored on the same cropped windows.

Accuracy is the 7-variable aggregate MSE and MAE in standardised space, averaged over channels and windows, reported per horizon and as a four-horizon mean. Peak skill de-normalises ILITOTAL to patient counts and measures, per season, the peak-timing error (PTE, weeks) and the peak-intensity error (PIE, % of the observed peak), at fixed steps 0/1/2/3 = 1/2/3/4 weeks ahead. A cell passes only if PTE <= 1 week and PIE <= 25 %. The thresholds are attributed to Kramer & Shaman (2019) and are marked [to verify] against the original text; peak detection (find_peaks(prominence = 0.15 x range, distance = 15), ±8-week matching) is this study's engineering choice, not part of the published criterion.

Every model selects its checkpoint on the validation block. The author's code selects on the test set (main_ILI_lora.py, lines 211 and 225); that is data leakage and is not replicated. The deviation is disclosed wherever a reproduction number appears.

Paired comparisons use exact sign-flip tests on the 12 matched (horizon x seed) cells, with Holm-Bonferroni correction over all 136 pairs of the 17 non-encoder arms (MIFlu and the 11 encoders are outside this family), a bootstrap 95 % CI (10,000 resamples), and Cohen's d. All arms share the same three seeds, which is what makes the 12 cells matched; with n = 12 the smallest attainable p is 2/2¹² ≈ 0.00049, and we state that floor rather than hide it. 128 of 136 pairs are significant before correction; after proper Holm none survives, because the smallest attainable adjusted p is 0.066.

The 204 cells of the 17 arms (13 conventional, 3 published LLM-based, and DLinear) ran on an A100-SXM4-80GB in the stingy partition of CityU HPC Burgundy, with GPU model, partition, node and job id recorded per cell; the MIFlu and encoder cells ran on the same partition with per-cell manifests on the cluster. Twelve NLinear cells were first measured on a V100-SXM2-32GB and re-run on A100; the two agree to 1e-6, so no ranking depends on the hardware. No timing claim is made anywhere in this paper.

Four analyses are reported, in this order. Reproduction (Table I): ten repetitions at four horizons against the published values. Accuracy (Table II): 28 arms x four horizons x three seeds, ranked by the four-horizon mean. Peak skill (Tables III-IV): the Kramer & Shaman criterion, per fixed step, on de-normalised patient counts. Efficiency and significance (Tables V-VI): a Pareto frontier and a log-parameter regression, then Holm-corrected paired tests. A fifth axis — frozen LLM encoders (Table VII) — and the ablation ladder (Table VIII) complete the matrix; the ladder is in progress and is reported as a design, not as a result.

The four-horizon mean is 1.4995 against the published 1.4355, i.e. 4.5 % worse, and the per-horizon sign flips: better at L=24 (1.3045 vs 1.542) and L=36 (1.3561 vs 1.422), worse at L=48 (1.6543 vs 1.414) and L=60 (1.6829 vs 1.364). The MAE side behaves the same way (0.8043 against 0.7452, +7.9 %). Reporting only the mean would have hidden the structure. Two explanations remain consistent with the pattern — validation-based checkpoint selection, and long-horizon variance (the ten repetitions span 1.401-1.984 at L=60) — and the data cannot yet separate them.
TABLE I. Reproduction of MIFlu's Table V — the sign crossover. 7-variable aggregate MSE in z-space, 10 repetitions, seeds 2021–2030.

A positive Δ means we are worse than the paper. We win L24 (−15.4 %) and L36 (−4.6 %) and lose L48 (+17.0 %) and L60 (+23.4 %); the 4-horizon mean is +4.5 % on MSE and +7.9 % on MAE. The only defensible claim is “reproduced within 4.5 % on the 4-horizon MSE mean, with a horizon-dependent sign” — never a claim of superiority over the original. Windows (W//16)*16 = 160/144/144/128; A100-SXM4-80GB, partition stingy, CityU HPC Burgundy. Source: ESSAY_VS_REPRODUCTION_TABLE_V.csv.

Takeaway. The reproduction is a reproduction, not an improvement: 4.5 % on the four-horizon mean, with a sign that depends on the horizon. The two disclosed deviations mean the per-horizon wins cannot be claimed as superiority over the original.

MIFlu is the accuracy champion at 1.5574, followed by PatchTST (1.6621) and NLinear (1.8716); the spread across all 28 arms is 1.5574 to 5.6155, a factor of 3.6, and all 28 beat the seasonal-naive reference (6.2132). The two published LLM-based forecasters are beaten by a nearest-neighbour baseline (KNN 3.7854 against Qwen-Time 5.2557 and CALF 5.5785). A linear model with 2,520 parameters is third of 28, ahead of every transformer except PatchTST.
